message.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has, over the past two decades, evolved [from {a (theoretically [grounded {and largely computational}] discipline)}] into a paradigm that permeates virtually every domain of human inquiry, from genomics to jurisprudence to the arts. The present paper situates itself within this broader trajectory, examining the [epistemological (and, {crucially, [methodological {and ethical}]})} implications of large-scale neural architectures as they increasingly mediate the production, verification, and dissemination of scholarly knowledge.

This is not, however, merely a technical critique. As {Bender (2021) [argues {that} (language models {are, [in the final analytical sense], *systems of* statistical recombination]}]}} has noted, the ontological status of "intelligence" as instantiated in these systems remains contested across at least four philosophical traditions. What is not contested, we submit, is the institutional pressure to deploy such systems in contexts—peer review, grant adjudication, curriculum design—where the stakes of error are non-trivial and the accountability structures are, to date, largely absent.

We therefore propose a three-part analytical framework: (i) a taxonomy of the [cognitive {functions (currently [offloaded {onto} automated pipelines] in research workflows)}]; (ii) a comparative audit of disclosure norms across four disciplinary communities; and (iii) a set of governance recommendations framed not as prescriptive regulation but as {adaptive {and, [deliberately, (revisable {over time})]}} policy. The remainder of this paper proceeds as follows: Section 2 reviews the literature; Section 3 details methodology; Section 4 presents findings; and Section 5 discusses limitations and avenues for future work.
